newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Cholera epidemic in Guinea-Bissau easing, WHO says.
newsitem.headline: Cholera epidemic in Guinea-Bissau easing, WHO says.

text.p: A cholera outbreak in the West African state of Guinea-Bissau which has killed 383 people is being brought under control, the World Health Organisation (WHO) said on Thursday.

Health ministry officials in the former Portuguese colony of Guinea-Bissau, one of the poorest countries in the world, said this week that 16,868 cases had been reported since authorities declared an epidemic last October.
"The situation is now more or less under control," Maria Neira, a global coordinator for cholera, told Reuters in a telephone interview from WHO headquarters in Geneva.

"As the rainy season ends soon and because a number of preventative steps have been taken, I expect the number of new cholera cases to start falling in the coming weeks," added Neira, who visited Guinea-Bissau last month.
Most of the cases registered so far were in and near the capital Bissau.

The city contains a quarter of the one million population of the flat and swampy country wedged between Senegal and Guinea. Sanitary conditions are basic for much of the population, who do not have lavatories.
Neira said that the capital suffered most because the bacteria was transmitted easily in crowds.
The disease had receded early this year and erupted again after the start of the rainy season in April.
But recent public health education campaigns and a distribution of free chlorine to purify water were improving the situation, Neira said.
The WHO has a permanent representative, sanitary engineer and health education specialist, as well as two doctors working in Bissau to bring the epidemic under control, she added.
It has made financial contributions to the public health education campaigns.

Neira said it was essential that the authorities took medium- and long-term steps to prevent further cholera outbreaks by upgrading the water distribution and sewage systems, as well as continuing the public health education programmes.
"Many people in Guinea-Bissau are still not taking basic steps such as washing their hands," she said.
"One problem is funerals, where the person who treats the body also prepares food for those attending the event, causing the bacteria to spread," she added.
The previous cholera epidemic in Guinea-Bissau, which lasted from October 1994 to March 1995, killed 290 people.
Cholera, spread by poor hygiene or the contamination of drinking water by sewage, brings on severe diarrhoea and dehydration and kills if not treated quickly.
Neira said hospitals in Guinea-Bissau were adequately equipped to treat the epidemic, but many victims had been taken there too late to be saved.
